title: Introduction
overview: Self-Mastery I is presented as a course in developing skills, rather than collecting explanations. Gary asks you to notice your attention, perspective, thoughts, emotions, body posture, and what he calls personal power: the conviction you invest in your interpretations. Early exercises work on small, ordinary reactions so later work has a foundation. The introductory material also explains why resistance, forgetting, and delayed awareness are part of the learning process. Begin by choosing a personally meaningful direction and a repeatable place for practice. You do not need to master an exercise before exploring the next one; the skills are intended to strengthen each other over time.
outcomes: Explain why reading and practicing are different kinds of learning.
Name the aspects of experience the course asks you to observe.
Choose a realistic practice opportunity and a personal learning intention.

concepts.title: A course in skills
concepts.explanation: The introduction distinguishes knowing an idea from being able to use it in a live situation. You can understand the instruction to notice your attention while still forgetting it during a busy day. Repetition is therefore the work, not evidence that you failed to understand. The space between lessons was designed for trying the practices in ordinary life. This site makes every week available, but the course’s original pacing rationale still matters: allow experience to accompany information.

concepts.title: Six things to notice
concepts.explanation: Gary directs attention toward thoughts, emotions, body posture, perspective, attention itself, and personal power. These are connected but not interchangeable. What you are thinking about differs from the attitude through which you view it; a bodily contraction differs from the sentence you tell yourself. The course’s language of personal power refers to the force of belief or conviction behind interpretations. At first simply distinguish these aspects in a recent event without trying to explain or change everything.

concepts.title: Retrospective awareness counts
concepts.explanation: You may first notice a reaction only while writing about it later. The introduction explicitly treats that as useful learning. Looking back lets you observe details you missed in the moment, and the course aims to make this noticing more available during future situations. Avoid making real-time awareness the entry requirement for practicing awareness. A useful study question is what you can see now that you could not see while the event was unfolding.

concepts.title: Small practices prepare larger changes
concepts.explanation: The course begins with manageable exercises because a strong emotional reaction may require several skills at once. Learning to move attention, question a thought, or shift perspective in a small situation develops the parts of that larger ability. Gary cautions against the urgency that demands a dramatic result immediately and then judges slow progress. His prediction that practice can produce larger changes is a teaching rationale, not a deadline or guarantee for your own experience.

concepts.title: Resistance becomes material
concepts.explanation: Boredom, postponement, doubt, and criticism may appear when an exercise interrupts a familiar habit. The introduction encourages noticing those responses and eventually applying the practices to them. This does not mean every concern is invalid or that you must force yourself through discomfort. It means the reaction to learning is itself something you can observe. A concrete sentence about what interrupted practice is more useful than a global verdict about being disciplined or undisciplined.

visual.intro: A study illustration of the course’s learning framework.

steps.label: Understand
steps.detail: Read or listen closely enough to know what the practice asks.

steps.label: Try
steps.detail: Use one small exercise in an ordinary situation.

steps.label: Notice
steps.detail: Observe thoughts, feelings, posture, attention, and perspective.

steps.label: Review
steps.detail: Write about what happened, including what you noticed later.

steps.label: Repeat
steps.detail: Let repeated attempts inform the next practice.

visual.takeaway: Knowing the instruction starts the process; repeated experience develops the skill.

practice.title: Set your intention and make room for practice
practice.cadence: The introduction recommends regular practice and deciding in advance when you will practice the following day. It does not prescribe one daily duration for the entire course.

steps.title: Read the orientation
steps.body: Read the introduction and distinguish its practice guidance from historical access and email details. Lessons in this library are available now; the original time gating was intended to protect practice time.

steps.title: Write a personal direction
steps.body: List what you want to understand or change. Keep these as your intentions rather than promised outcomes. Ask how greater awareness of attention, perspective, emotion, or conviction might support that direction.

steps.title: Choose a repeatable opportunity
steps.body: Decide when tomorrow’s practice will fit. The course suggests making this as predictable as familiar daily routines, so you do not have to rediscover a time late at night.

steps.title: Start with an ordinary experience
steps.body: Briefly recall something from today. Name a thought, an emotion, a bodily sensation or posture, where attention went, and the perspective involved. This is a study adaptation of the introduction’s observation targets.

steps.title: Record resistance accurately
steps.body: If your mind demands faster results, predicts failure, or wants more information before doing anything, note the actual thought. Treat it as information for later lessons rather than a conclusion about yourself.

steps.title: Carry practice forward
steps.body: Begin Week 1 and return to earlier exercises as later skills develop. Do not require flawless performance before continuing, and do not treat finishing a page as completing the practice.

prompts: What do I want to be more able to notice or choose in daily life?
What specific opportunity will I use for practice tomorrow?
In one recent moment, where was my attention and from what perspective was I looking?
What expectation about progress might make learning harder?

obstacles.title: I want the next insight immediately
obstacles.response: The introduction asks you to connect small practices to your larger intention and to allow time for integration. Repeated practice is purposeful, even when the instruction is already familiar.

obstacles.title: I only noticed after the event
obstacles.response: The orientation explicitly values reflective noticing. Write what you now see; that is part of developing awareness.

obstacles.title: I missed a day
obstacles.response: Choose the next concrete practice opportunity. The introduction’s scheduling suggestion is more actionable than arguing with a critical story about the missed day.

stories.title: The first day at the gym
stories.summary: Gary compares approaching inner change to arriving at a gym and immediately trying to bench-press 300 pounds. Such a beginning sets up an avoidable struggle. Training begins with manageable weights and many repetitions, gradually building capacity. He applies the analogy to beliefs and emotional reactions: practice with small ones before expecting to change the most powerful patterns. The image also challenges a common measure of success. A small exercise is not insignificant simply because the desired life change is large. Its value lies in developing an ability that can be used again.
stories.lesson: Choose a workable repetition rather than using the size of your goal as today’s performance demand.

stories.title: Listening like a musician
stories.summary: The second introductory handout compares awareness to a musician listening for individual instruments and noticing how their sounds work together or cancel each other. A listener who only hears a single mass of sound may miss those relationships. Likewise, the learner begins to distinguish thoughts, emotions, posture, perspective, and attention within an experience that previously felt like one reaction. Gary uses the comparison to explain why an intellectual definition of awareness cannot substitute for practicing this discrimination in actual experience.
stories.lesson: Learn to distinguish the components of experience without immediately judging the whole performance.

storiesNote: These are teaching metaphors in the introductory handouts, paraphrased for study.

cheatsheet.principle: Practice builds the ability to use what you understand.
remember: Observe attention, perspective, thoughts, emotions, body posture, and conviction.
Noticing later is still noticing.
Begin with small, manageable situations.
Earlier exercises continue to support later ones.
Choose tomorrow’s practice opportunity in advance.
cheatsheet.try: Write one intention and one specific time or routine for your next practice.
cheatsheet.watchFor: Turning urgency for change into an impossible deadline.
cheatsheet.question: What is the difference between knowing an exercise and being able to use it?

quiz.question: You recognize a reaction only while journaling that evening. According to the introduction, this is…
options: Too late to be useful
A useful part of training awareness
Proof you should skip to harder material
quiz.explanation: Reflective awareness is explicitly described as valuable preparation for noticing during events.

quiz.question: Why do the early exercises focus on relatively small changes?
options: They develop skills that combine in later work
The course says major concerns do not matter
You must perfect one skill before learning another
quiz.explanation: The introductory rationale is progressive skill development, with practices supporting one another.

reflection: What did I notice that I usually overlook?
What made the practice easier to begin?
What small adjustment would make another attempt more realistic?

title: Gratitude
overview: Week 1 asks you to practice directing attention toward what supports your life and, where possible, expressing gratitude as a feeling. The exercise combines attention, interpretation, perspective, and emotion. In Gary’s house metaphor, this begins building a more supportive place from which to examine old beliefs later. Gratitude is therefore both a practice in its own right and preparation for the rest of the course. The daily journal is especially important when a grateful feeling is difficult to access: you can still notice a concrete benefit without pretending to feel something. Ordinary moments, repeated frequently, are the intended setting for much of this work.
outcomes: Explain gratitude’s role in the course beyond making a list.
Practice directing attention toward a specific benefit and observe the result honestly.
Keep a daily gratitude entry without demanding a particular emotional response.

concepts.title: Attention, viewpoint, and emotion
concepts.explanation: The written practice describes gratitude as changing what you attend to, the point of view you occupy, and the dialogue in your mind together. A familiar object can be seen as an inconvenience, an entitlement, or something that helps you live. The exercise explores that change in interpretation. It does not require denying difficulties. You are learning to notice an available channel of appreciation alongside the other things occurring in your life.

concepts.title: An emotional home for later work
concepts.explanation: The lesson compares entrenched beliefs to the walls of a house. Some once seemed to offer protection, even when their present effects are costly. Pulling them apart can feel threatening. Gary presents gratitude as a way to develop another emotional standpoint before examining those older structures. Read this as the course’s metaphor for preparation: cultivate a supportive capacity, rather than attacking every difficult pattern at once or expecting one positive feeling to erase it.

concepts.title: Expression rather than a correct answer
concepts.explanation: In the guided lesson, gratitude is something you direct toward the body, a person, an experience, a meal, shelter, or another concrete support. The words and the list provide an entry point, but the invitation is also to notice the felt expression. A long list is not automatically a deeper practice. If a single everyday benefit invites attention and appreciation, it can be enough material for one attempt.

concepts.title: Writing is a valid starting point
concepts.explanation: The practice guide explicitly accommodates difficulty creating a feeling of gratitude. You can write what benefited you or made life easier even when the emotion is faint or absent. This keeps the exercise honest and workable. Repeating the same items initially is also allowed; the guide suggests perception may widen through practice. The useful observation is what you actually notice, not whether your entry looks original, uplifting, or impressive to anyone else.

concepts.title: Repetition under ordinary conditions
concepts.explanation: The supporting guidance contrasts knowing how to do a push-up with developing the strength to repeat it, and making one basketball shot with performing under pressure. In the same way, a moment of gratitude is a beginning rather than proof of permanent mastery. The brief practices throughout the day develop familiarity. Boredom and distraction can be noted without turning the entire course into a race to acquire the next piece of information.

visual.title: The gratitude practice cycle
visual.intro: A study illustration of the course’s gratitude exercise, not a claim that emotion changes on command.

steps.label: Notice a support
steps.detail: Choose something specific that helps or enriches your life.

steps.label: See its benefit
steps.detail: Attend to what it makes possible instead of taking it for granted.

steps.label: Express appreciation
steps.detail: Direct gratitude toward it if that feeling is available.

steps.label: Observe honestly
steps.detail: Notice feeling, attention, and inner dialogue without forcing them.

steps.label: Write and revisit
steps.detail: Record the benefit and return to practice during the day.

visual.takeaway: A concrete observation is useful even when a strong feeling does not arrive.

practice.title: Practice and journal gratitude
practice.cadence: Practice periodically during the day and write daily. The guide permits very brief moments, a few minutes, or a longer focused meditation; it gives examples of 3 seconds, 3 minutes, or 30 minutes rather than a required duration.

steps.title: Study the lesson
steps.body: Read or listen to the gratitude lesson, returning to it if useful. Notice the distinction between constructing a list and practicing a shift in attention and feeling.

steps.title: Choose a concrete focus
steps.body: Select a person, experience, bodily capacity, everyday object, or practical support that you can honestly appreciate. Begin with what is accessible rather than what you think ought to impress you.

steps.title: Attend to what it provides
steps.body: Consider what this support makes possible. The lesson moves through the body, senses, shelter, food, work, and the people whose contributions make everyday life possible.

steps.title: Invite the expression
steps.body: If comfortable, relax and let your breathing accompany appreciation. The lesson uses breathing gratitude through the body and outward as an imaginative aid. Treat this as imagery, not a physical mechanism you must reproduce.

steps.title: Return during the day
steps.body: Try small moments while doing ordinary tasks or waiting. Use a safe pause when an activity requires your full attention; the practice can be brief and need not interrupt necessary action.

steps.title: Write the daily entry
steps.body: Record what you are grateful for or what supported your life today. If little emotion is present, say so. The guide values the writing and change of focus even before the feeling becomes accessible.

steps.title: Notice resistance
steps.body: Write down boredom, distraction, or the demand for a larger result when it appears. Return to a manageable repetition rather than criticizing the lack of a dramatic experience.

prompts: What specific thing helped me today, and how?
What did I notice in my attention, body, or mood while appreciating it?
Who contributed to an ordinary benefit I usually take for granted?
If I did not feel gratitude, what benefit could I still honestly acknowledge?

obstacles.title: I cannot create the feeling
obstacles.response: Use the writing portion and name concrete benefits. Do not pretend an emotion occurred. The source explicitly allows beginning with thoughts and perspective.

obstacles.title: My list is repetitive
obstacles.response: The guide says repetition is common at first. Give a familiar item specific attention rather than making novelty the success criterion.

obstacles.title: This seems too simple
obstacles.response: The house and training metaphors explain the intended long-term role. Observe the actual experience of a small practice before deciding that simplicity makes it irrelevant.

stories.title: Building a second house
stories.summary: The lesson imagines the belief system as a house whose walls include protective habits such as anger or seeking help through helplessness. Even when those habits become costly, dismantling them from inside can feel like losing shelter. Gary describes three approaches: observing the old house, building another place to live emotionally, and taking apart the old structures. Gratitude belongs to building the second house. It offers another viewpoint and emotional experience from which the older habits can eventually be examined. The metaphor links a simple gratitude exercise to the course’s later belief work without claiming the old house disappears in one session.
stories.lesson: Cultivate a supportive standpoint before demanding that deeply familiar patterns vanish.

stories.title: The many people inside one meal
stories.summary: During the guided exercise Gary widens attention from the meal itself to the people who made it possible. Someone may have cooked or served it; a farmer grew ingredients; a driver transported them; other people built the place where the meal is eaten. An ordinary experience becomes a network of contributions. The point is not to produce an exhaustive list or compare your life competitively with someone else’s. It is to notice supports that are easy to overlook and to direct appreciation toward them. The exercise then returns to daily activities as opportunities for another brief expression.
stories.lesson: Look beyond the most visible benefit to the contributions supporting it.

storiesNote: The supporting One Week to Live video adds a reflection on limited time and priorities. It is a perspective exercise, not a prediction or a requirement to dwell on mortality.

cheatsheet.principle: Practice appreciation by directing attention to an actual benefit.
remember: Gratitude involves viewpoint and expression, not only a list.
Use ordinary supports: food, shelter, senses, people, and experiences.
Brief repetitions count.
Write daily even when emotion is faint.
Keep observations honest; do not manufacture a success report.
cheatsheet.try: Pause with one ordinary object and name exactly how it helps your life.
cheatsheet.watchFor: Treating difficulty feeling gratitude as another reason to judge yourself.
cheatsheet.question: What can you practice when the feeling of gratitude is not available?

quiz.question: You recognize something helpful but feel little gratitude. What does the guide recommend?
options: Stop until the emotion arrives
Write about the benefit and continue gently
Claim that you feel grateful anyway
quiz.explanation: The written practice allows beginning with thought and perspective through journaling.

quiz.question: In the house metaphor, gratitude mainly helps you…
options: Prove every old belief false immediately
Build a supportive standpoint for later examination
Avoid examining beliefs forever
quiz.explanation: The second house provides a different emotional viewpoint from which old structures can be explored.

quiz.question: Why repeat a simple practice during the week?
options: Repetition develops a usable skill
New information is forbidden
A single missed attempt cancels the earlier ones
quiz.explanation: The supporting guidance distinguishes knowing an exercise from having practiced its use.

reflection: Which ordinary support became more visible this week?
What changed, if anything, between listing a benefit and attending to it?
What small practice could I keep as the next week begins?
coverageNote: The main handout and written lesson provide the exercise and guided meditation. Supporting videos add the one-week-to-live perspective and the distinction between knowing and training. Physiological explanations in the original are not used here as established medical facts.

title: Abdication of Power
overview: This week examines the stories through which you attribute an emotional response entirely to another person or circumstance. Gary calls this abdication: treating the power over your feelings as if it belongs outside you. The practice is to notice the wording, acknowledge your interpretation or agreement, and rewrite the account more precisely. This is a first step in examining beliefs, not a demand to eliminate a reaction immediately. The written guide also makes a crucial distinction: other people remain accountable for their behavior. Investigating your internal response does not require excusing harmful actions, staying in an unwanted situation, or taking blame for what someone else did.
outcomes: Distinguish an external event from your interpretation of it.
Identify an explicit or implied statement that assigns emotional power externally.
Rewrite a reaction account to include your beliefs without removing others’ accountability.

concepts.title: Event and interpretation are different
concepts.explanation: The guide’s traffic example separates a careless lane change from interpretations such as danger, recklessness, or a demand for punishment. Gary asks you to notice the part played by beliefs in the emotional sequence. Two people may react differently to the same event, and you may react differently on another day. This is a prompt to investigate your contribution to experience, not evidence that circumstances have no consequences or that all emotion is a consciously chosen thought.

concepts.title: The shorthand hides a model
concepts.explanation: Phrases such as another person making you angry can compress an entire explanation into a few familiar words. The lesson asks what you are assuming when you use that shorthand. Are you treating your response as inevitable? Are you overlooking an expectation or interpretation? Naming that assumption can reveal a possible area for change. The assignment includes speech, inner commentary, and an emotional reaction whose explanation has not yet been put into words.

concepts.title: Power goes into agreements
concepts.explanation: Gary clarifies that no literal substance or force has been transferred to the other person. In his model, conviction has been invested in an agreement about what their action means and how you must respond. The other person may activate that agreement, but they do not possess a piece of you that must be retrieved. The practical implication is to look at your assumptions and commitments rather than wait for the other person to change before examining your own response.

concepts.title: Responsibility includes boundaries
concepts.explanation: The main handout explicitly preserves accountability for others’ actions. A supporting talk also describes choosing not to live with, spend time with, or accept mistreatment from someone. These distinctions prevent the practice from becoming self-blame. You can investigate your interpretation while naming what happened accurately and taking protective or practical action. The study task is to find agency in your response, not to declare that you caused someone else’s behavior.

concepts.title: Acknowledge before correcting
concepts.explanation: The lesson warns against instantly denying or dismissing the statement you caught. First acknowledge that this is what you thought or said, and see the agreement it implies. Then rewrite it to include your own beliefs or interpretation. At this stage, the assignment changes where you look for the emotional mechanism; it does not require that every underlying belief dissolve. Observing the mind is more useful here than forcing it to stop thinking.

visual.title: Unpack the reaction
visual.intro: A study illustration of Gary’s framework; it highlights interpretation without reducing every emotion to this single sequence.

steps.label: Event
steps.detail: Describe what happened in observable terms.

steps.label: Interpretation
steps.detail: Notice what your mind says the event means.

steps.label: Agreement
steps.detail: Look for an expectation, assumption, or conviction you treated as true.

steps.label: Response
steps.detail: Name emotion, bodily response, and action separately.

steps.label: Reframe
steps.detail: Include your internal contribution while keeping the event and accountability clear.

visual.takeaway: Change the account from an inevitable external cause to an inquiry into the response.

practice.title: Catch and rewrite abdication statements
practice.cadence: Watch thoughts and speech during the day and spend some time journaling daily. The guide illustrates the cumulative value of noticing often; it does not make hourly perfection a requirement.

steps.title: Study the lesson
steps.body: Read or listen to the main lesson. Notice the difference between an external stimulus, the belief about it, and the emotion that follows.

steps.title: Catch the wording
steps.body: Look for phrases that make a person, object, schedule, or circumstance the sole author of your emotion. Also notice the implied rule that you can only feel differently after something outside you changes.

steps.title: Acknowledge the observation
steps.body: Record what you actually said or thought. Do not replace the evidence with a polished story of how you think you ought to respond.

steps.title: Describe the event separately
steps.body: Write a concise account of what occurred. Keep it distinct from the meanings your mind supplied, such as disrespect, danger, rejection, or unfairness.

steps.title: Name your contribution
steps.body: Identify an interpretation, expectation, or belief if you can. A course-style reframe includes that you are having an emotion through your beliefs about the event. If the belief is unclear, record the uncertainty rather than inventing one.

steps.title: Retain practical responsibility
steps.body: Identify any action, boundary, or communication still needed. The exercise does not remove the other person’s responsibility or require you to remain in a harmful or unwanted interaction.

steps.title: Review without demanding instant change
steps.body: Write the original statement and the revised account in your journal. Notice whether your viewpoint changes; do not require the emotion to disappear for the observation to count.

prompts: What did my mind say caused this emotion?
What happened, and what meaning did I add to it?
What expectation or agreement can I actually identify?
How can I include my interpretation in the account without blaming myself for another person’s action?
What practical action or boundary remains relevant?

obstacles.title: This feels like excusing someone else
obstacles.response: The written guide distinguishes their accountability from your emotional process. Keep both in view rather than using one to erase the other.

obstacles.title: I want to stop the blaming thoughts
obstacles.response: The guide says observing the mind is useful at this stage. Catching and writing the thought provides material for later belief work.

obstacles.title: I understand the reframe but still feel upset
obstacles.response: The lesson states that locating power in agreements is different from changing all those agreements. Observe the response and continue the practice without making immediate relief the test.

stories.title: Two people in the same snow
stories.summary: The written lesson imagines cold, snowy weather. One person experiences it as depressing, while another finds it beautiful and enjoyable. Gary uses the contrast to question the everyday statement that weather itself determines the same feeling in everyone. In his explanation, each person brings an agreement and a point of view to the event. The example is a teaching simplification about interpretation, not a claim that weather cannot affect bodies, plans, or health. Its useful question is narrower: what meaning am I adding, and am I treating that meaning as the only possible response?
stories.lesson: Notice the interpretation you bring to a circumstance before calling your reaction inevitable.

stories.title: A compliment with two meanings
stories.summary: The lesson describes how a compliment about appearance might feel flattering at one time and unconvincing or even uncomfortable at another. In the second case, a person may suspect the speaker is being dishonest or merely saying what they want to hear. The same type of words can meet different agreements and perspectives. Gary uses the example to show why praise does not operate like a mechanical emotional switch. For study, follow the meaning assigned to the compliment and the view of self involved, rather than trying to decide which response everyone should have.
stories.lesson: The meaning received can matter as much as the words delivered.

storiesNote: The supporting Accepting Responsibility talk includes Gary’s own relationship reflection and explicitly discusses setting boundaries. The examples above come from the written lesson.

cheatsheet.principle: Notice the event, then investigate the interpretation you brought to it.
remember: Catch speech, thoughts, and implied emotional rules.
Acknowledge what you actually thought before rewriting it.
Personal power is the course’s language for conviction invested in agreements.
A reframe is not the same as dissolving an underlying belief.
Other people remain accountable for their behavior.
cheatsheet.try: Write: event / my interpretation / emotion / a more precise account.
cheatsheet.watchFor: Replacing blame of others with blame of yourself, or using the practice to excuse mistreatment.
cheatsheet.question: What changes when you add “my beliefs about this” to an emotional explanation?

quiz.question: What is the main assignment this week?
options: Make every unpleasant emotion stop
Notice and reframe where you attribute emotional power
Prove other people never do harm
quiz.explanation: The assignment locates and questions agreements in the account of a reaction.

quiz.question: Does the exercise remove another person’s responsibility?
options: Yes, all responsibility becomes yours
No, their behavior and your internal response remain distinct
Only if you feel calmer
quiz.explanation: The main practice guide expressly says it is not taking responsibility away from others.

quiz.question: You catch an abdication statement. What comes first?
options: Pretend you never believed it
Acknowledge it and examine its implied agreement
Argue until the emotion disappears
quiz.explanation: The written lesson cautions against denying or dismissing what you just noticed.

reflection: Which repeated phrase most clearly hid an assumption?
Where did a more precise account create even a little room for choice?
How did I distinguish self-inquiry from self-blame?
